summary: Defines common semantics and data formats for instant messaging to make it easier to build gateways between services. Many instant messaging protocols existed, and this profile gives a shared model for sending messages between them.

plainLanguage.summary: Instant messaging services in the early 2000s rarely talked to each other. CPIM gives them a common set of operations and a common address format, so a gateway can pass a message from one service to another without reading it. It also fixes the way a message is formatted, which lets a message stay protected from end to end.

questions: what is the im uri scheme
subtitle: A shared abstract model for instant messages, so gateways can connect different messaging services.

tldr.problem: Numerous instant messaging protocols were in use and little interoperability between the services built on them had been achieved.
tldr.mechanism: CPIM defines abstract message and response operations, im: addresses, a hop counter against loops and a common end-to-end message format, so gateways can relay content between services.
tldr.outcome: A protocol that supports each operation can interface with CPIM gateways, and secure messages can keep their end-to-end protection through them by using the common message format with S/MIME.

today: RFC 3860 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It remains the common profile that instant messaging gateways were built against.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Instant messaging is defined in RFC 2778. Numerous instant messaging protocols were in use at the time this document was written, and little interoperability between services based on those protocols had been achieved. This specification defines semantics and data formats for the common services of instant messaging, so that gateways between those services can be created: a common profile for instant messaging, or CPIM.

Service behavior is described abstractly, in terms of operations invoked between the consumer and the provider of a service. Each instant messaging service must specify how that behavior maps onto its own protocol interactions, and the choice of strategy is a local matter, provided the mapping is clear. One strategy might transmit an instant message as textual key and value pairs, another might use a compact binary representation, and a third might use nested containers.

The attributes for each operation are defined using an abstract syntax. Although the syntax specifies the range of possible data values, each service must specify how well-formed instances of the abstract representation are encoded as a concrete series of bits.
sections.plainLanguage: CPIM does not define a new messaging protocol. It defines the operations any messaging protocol must support if it wants to be connected to a gateway, and leaves the wire format to each protocol.

sections.title: Overview of the Messaging Service
sections.content:
When an application wants to send a message to an instant inbox, it invokes the message operation. That operation has the following attributes: source, destination, MaxForwards and TransID. The source and the destination identify the originator and the recipient of the instant message and consist of an instant inbox identifier. The MaxForwards is a hop counter that avoids loops through gateways, with its initial value set by the originator. The TransID is a unique identifier used to correlate message operations with response operations, and gateways should be capable of handling TransIDs up to 40 bytes in length.

The message operation also carries content, the instant message itself, which may be textual or may consist of other data. The specification assumes that instant messaging protocols provide reliable message delivery, so there are no application-layer message delivery assurance provisions in it.

Upon receiving a message operation, the service responds immediately by invoking the response operation with the same transaction identifier. The response operation carries the TransID and a status, where the status indicates whether delivery of the message succeeded or failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a message means handing it to a messaging service with a sender, a recipient, a loop counter and a transaction number. The service answers straight away with the same transaction number and a status saying whether it worked.

sections.title: Identifying an Instant Inbox
sections.content:
An instant inbox is specified using an instant messaging URI with the im: URI scheme. The full syntax of the IM URI scheme is given in the appendix of the RFC, and an example is im:fred@example.com.

An instant messaging service client determines the next hop to forward the message to by resolving the domain name portion of the service destination. Compliant implementations SHOULD follow the guidelines for dereferencing URIs given in RFC 3861.
sections.plainLanguage: An instant inbox is named like an email address but starts with im:. The part after the @ sign is a domain name, and the client looks that domain up to find out where to send the message next.

sections.title: Format of Instant Messages
sections.content:
This specification defines an abstract interoperability mechanism for instant messaging protocols. The message content definition given here pertains to semantics rather than syntax. However, some important properties for interoperability can only be provided if a common end-to-end format for instant messaging is employed by the interoperating protocols, especially with respect to security.

In order to maintain end-to-end security properties, applications that send message operations to a CPIM gateway MUST implement the format defined in the Common Presence and Instant Messaging message format document, RFC 3862. Applications MAY support other content formats. CPIM gateways MUST be capable of relaying the content of a message operation between supported instant messaging protocols without needing to modify or inspect the content.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway passes the message along without opening it. That only works if both sides use the same message format, so RFC 3860 requires one common format for messages that cross a gateway.

sections.title: The Message Operation
sections.content:
When an instant messaging service receives the message operation it performs three preliminary checks. If the source or the destination does not refer to a syntactically valid instant inbox, a response operation with status failure is invoked. If the destination cannot be resolved by the recipient and the recipient is not the final recipient, a response operation with status failure is invoked. If access control does not permit the application to request the operation, a response operation with status failure is invoked.

Provided those checks succeed, the service invokes a response operation with status success if it is able to deliver the message, and one with status failure if it is unable to. If the service must delegate responsibility for delivery, because it is acting as a gateway or proxying the operation, and the delegation will not result in a future authoritative indication to the service, a response operation with status indeterminant is invoked. If the delegation will result in a future authoritative indication, then the response operation is invoked immediately after that indication is received.

When the service invokes the response operation, the TransID is identical to the value found in the message operation invoked by the application.
sections.plainLanguage: The service checks the addresses, checks that the sender is allowed to send, and then reports one of three outcomes: delivered, not delivered, or handed on to someone else with no answer yet.

sections.title: Looping
sections.content:
The dynamic routing of instant messages can result in a message looping through a relay. Detection of loops is not always obvious, since aliasing and group list expansions can legitimately cause a message to pass through a relay more than one time.

The document assumes that instant messaging protocols which can be gatewayed by CPIM support a semantic equivalent to an integer value indicating the maximum number of hops a message may pass through. When that number of hops has been reached, the message is assumed to have looped.

When a CPIM gateway relays an instant message, it decrements the value of the MaxForwards attribute. The document does not mandate any particular initial setting for MaxForwards in instant messaging protocols, but it is recommended that the value be reasonably large, over one hundred. If a CPIM gateway receives a message operation that has a MaxForwards attribute of 0, it discards the message and invokes a failure operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gateway that forwards a message lowers a counter by one. When the counter reaches zero the message is thrown away, so a message cannot circle between gateways forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Detailed security considerations for instant messaging protocols are given in RFC 2779. CPIM defines an interoperability function employed by gateways between instant messaging protocols, and CPIM gateways MUST be compliant with the minimum security requirements of the instant messaging protocols with which they interface.

The introduction of gateways to the security model of instant messaging in RFC 2779 also introduces new risks. End-to-end security properties, especially confidentiality and integrity, between instant messaging user agents that interface through a CPIM gateway can only be provided if a common instant message format, such as the format described in RFC 3862, is supported by the protocols interfacing with the gateway.

When end-to-end security is required, the message operation MUST use the RFC 3862 format and MUST secure its MIME body with S/MIME, using encryption in the CMS EnvelopeData form and or S/MIME signatures in the CMS SignedData form. The S/MIME algorithms are set by the Cryptographic Message Syntax. The AES algorithm should be preferred, as it is expected that AES best suits the capabilities of many platforms. Implementations MAY use AES as an encryption algorithm but are REQUIRED to support only the baseline algorithms mandated by S/MIME and CMS.

When IM URIs are placed in instant messaging protocols they convey the identity of the sender and or the recipient. Certificates used for S/MIME instant messaging operations SHOULD contain a subjectAltName field holding the IM URI of their subject, for the purposes of reference integrity. Users and service providers are encouraged to employ trust anchors for certificates that are widely accepted rather than trust anchors specific to any particular instant messaging service or provider. In some cases anonymous messaging may be desired, and that capability is beyond the scope of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A message that must stay private has to be encrypted and signed in the standard format, because a gateway can only pass a protected message on without breaking it. Anonymous messaging is left out of this RFC.

sections.title: The IM URI Scheme
sections.content:
The IANA has assigned the im scheme. The Instant Messaging URI scheme designates an Internet resource, namely an instant inbox, and its syntax follows the existing mailto URI syntax specified in RFC 2368. The ABNF given in the RFC is IM-URI = "im:" [ to ] [ headers ], where to = mailbox, headers = "?" header *( "&" header ), header = hname "=" hvalue, hname = *uric and hvalue = *uric. The symbol mailbox represents an encoded mailbox name as defined in RFC 2822, and uric denotes any character valid in a URL as defined in RFC 2396.

Use of the im URI follows the usage of the mailto URI closely: invoking an IM URI causes the user's instant messaging application to start, with the destination address and message headers filled in from the information in the URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The im: scheme is a small syntax borrowed from mailto:, so that an instant messaging address can be put in a web page or a message and start the right program.

viz.caption: THE MESSAGE AND RESPONSE OPERATIONS AS DRAWN IN RFC 3860

messages.label: MESSAGE OPERATION
messages.note: Carries source, destination, MaxForwards, TransID and the message content.

messages.label: RESPONSE OPERATION
messages.note: Carries the same TransID and a status saying whether delivery succeeded.

viz.caption: THE THREE STATUS VALUES A RESPONSE OPERATION MAY CARRY

items.label: DELIVERED
items.desc: The service delivered the message itself.

items.label: NOT DELIVERED
items.desc: The service could not deliver the message, or a preliminary check failed.

items.label: HANDED ON
items.desc: The service delegated delivery and will not receive an authoritative answer later.

viz.caption: THE ABNF FOR THE im: URI AS PRINTED IN RFC 3860

data.title: IM-URI
data.code:
IM-URI         = "im:" [ to ] [ headers ]
   to             =  mailbox
   headers        =  "?" header *( "&" header )
   header         =  hname "=" hvalue
   hname          =  *uric
   hvalue         =  *uric
